store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theory behind real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class dives into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor is excellent at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She presents a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time and then shows us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with new ideas and insights.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, my other challenging class this semester is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It's a lot of reading and group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with team members who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about the final product. However, this diversity is also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in isolation. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures effectively. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.8: I also have to mention my Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced for me. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is some math involved, such as linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. store.10: My Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all the agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
